Evans calls it a contract. The writer promises the facts as she remembers them, and the emotional truth underneath them. Both sides accept that memory fails, and that two people can carry different versions of the same afternoon.

A memoir also reaches past one life. It usually has a wider point, often a political one. Hers is about her own losses and, at the same time, an investigation into the British tabloid press — the story most people remember as phone hacking, which she says was a police corruption scandal at heart.

sections.label: How much is the writer allowed to invent?
sections.text:
Reading Angelou and Tara Westover, Evans kept getting stuck on one question: how does anyone remember which way the wind was blowing? Then she started writing. She closed her eyes, and her own mind handed the details back — a pigeon pecking at the paving, her fingernail picking at flaky paint on a bench. She could not swear that each one was exact. It simply felt like being there again.

So she drew the line somewhere else. A blurry memory is not a lie. Emotional truth is not permission to invent facts.

sections.label: Why does this fall harder on women?
sections.text: Memoir leaves a writer more open to shame than any other kind of book, Evans says. And the doubt falls unevenly. Readers ask whether a woman was a good daughter, a good mother, whether she behaved as they think she should — and that judgment quietly turns into a judgment about whether she is telling the truth. Westover’s own family are the ones disputing her account.

sections.label: Which five memoirs taught her the most?
items: The Rules Do Not Apply, Ariel Levy — Levy loses a baby at 19 weeks and her marriage in the same stretch of life. Evans, who lost a baby at 27 weeks, found it the book that finally made her feel understood. She also saw the craft: Levy builds a scene from one or two details instead of piling them up.

Educated, Tara Westover — a strict Mormon childhood in Idaho, escaped through study. It reads so much like a novel that Evans began asking how much of any memoir is there because it happened, and how much because it helps the story.

I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings, Maya Angelou — a girlhood spent with her grandmother in the American South of the 1930s and 40s. Its power is not exact detail. It is the force of the voice and the moral truth inside it.

A Life of My Own, Claire Tomalin — a famous biographer of Dickens turns the same cool eye on her own life, with no self-pity: a daughter’s suicide, a husband killed while working as a foreign correspondent, a profoundly disabled son, a long newspaper career, and no speech anywhere about her own strength.

The Salt Path, Raynor Winn — a couple in their 50s lose their home and their money, then walk the South West Coast Path with backpacks while the husband’s illness slowly gets worse. Beautifully written, and now in dispute.

sections.label: And the question nobody can settle?
sections.text:
The Salt Path is the hard case. The Observer investigated and raised serious questions about how the couple lost their home. Winn disputed the reporting, and her lawyers said the book is still the ‘true story of their journey.’ Evans does not think that settles it. If the main facts were changed so the writer looks blameless, the contract is broken. Forgetting a conversation is one thing. Cutting out your own bad choices is another.

She also thinks the honest version would have been worth reading: a story where someone owns the wrong can still end in forgiveness. Which leaves her interviewer’s question hanging in the air. Suppose a memoirist wrote that she got into trouble because she stole some money — would a publisher have wanted that book? No memoir can answer that about itself.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Memory is allowed to be wrong. The writer is not allowed to know better and write it anyway.

recall.q: Evans accepts that a memoirist may not truly remember which way the wind was blowing. So what does break the contract with the reader?
recall.a: Knowingly changing what happened — especially to make yourself look blameless. Faulty memory is expected, because the promise was only truth to the facts as you remember them.

cards.title: No one has published a Snowden document since 2019
cards.body: The last document from the Snowden archive came out on 29 May 2019. Full copies still exist — two journalists hold one each, and one sits locked in an office at The New York Times. The people who hold them say important material is still unreported.

sections.text:
No document from the Snowden archive has been published since 29 May 2019 — not by a newspaper, not by a journalist, not by an institution. In 2013 Edward Snowden, a contractor inside American intelligence, gave reporters tens of thousands of secret files on mass surveillance. Five outlets published from them. All five stopped.

Where the files sit is clear. Glenn Greenwald and Laura Poitras each say they still hold full copies. One copy is locked in an office at The New York Times, with the Guardian still responsible for it. Other copies went to trusted people who may not even have the key.

How much was never published is not known. Asked how many of the Guardian's 58,000 documents had been read, its editor said he could not say. Nobody has explained why the publishing stopped.

The holders do not agree on what should happen now. Poitras says there is "still more to report". Barton Gellman says the files are useful for research, but the security work needed to share them is too much to take on. Ewen MacAskill blames falling reader interest — though the Guardian won a Pulitzer two months after its last document.

sections.label: The numbers
items: The Guardian: about 30 documents published out of the 58,000 it held — 0.05%
The Washington Post: about 30 documents, about 0.06% of the copy it held
Der Spiegel: about 140 documents across 18 stories — the biggest run by any outlet. It stopped in January 2015
Barton Gellman: more than 50,000 documents sitting in what he calls "cold storage"

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: This is the record of how states watched ordinary people, and almost none of it is public. The choice to keep it that way was never announced or argued anywhere. A handful of private people made it, and it has held for seven years.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: The Guardian's press office was asked three questions in August 2026: does it still hold a copy, is material still at The New York Times, and can it approve or block what its partners publish? It answered none of them. ProPublica did not reply. Three plain answers would show who controls the archive now.

recall.q: Ewen MacAskill says the silence is because readers lost interest. Which fact about the Guardian's own reporting argues against that?
recall.a: The Guardian won a Pulitzer for that reporting two months after it published its last document. Interest had not dried up, so the real reason for stopping is still unexplained — nobody holding the archive has given one.

cards.title: An essay written with AI, about being written with AI
cards.body: A writer builds his sentences in conversation with Claude and ChatGPT. He says so at the top of every column. His editor accepted one with a complaint attached: the sentences sound machine-made, but the ideas are clearly the writer's own. Both are true. That, he says, is why the question everyone asks — did AI write this? — settles nothing.

sections.text:
The message that accepted the column also complained about it.

An editor told Jeremy Moss that his prose "carries the unmistakable tone that AI-written material still carries." In the same message he said he fully believed the ideas were Moss's own, not Claude's, and wanted to run the column anyway. The sentences read as machine-made. The argument reads as a person's. Hold both, and you still have no verdict.

Moss calls his method Four Hands, after the piano duet: two players at one instrument, both parts printed in the score. He brings the ideas, the direction, and the final call on what stays. The sentences come out of conversation with Claude and ChatGPT, which he addresses together as Machina. He says all this at the top of every column, so it is settled before the first line instead of argued about after.

A piece starts as an itch, not a thesis — something he noticed across years of clinical work and cannot place, a question he would once have taken to his father. He puts it into the conversation. Some of what comes back is useless, and he says so. Even that is not wasted: the rejections build a shared sense of where not to go. More often than he expected, what comes back is his own thought handed to him with pressure on the weak part. Sometimes it changes the question instead of answering it. Then he goes again, inside everything already argued over and thrown out.

What he gets is not correctness. Alone, he says, you get stuck in your first version of the idea. You know what you mean, so every next sentence goes to defending it. The page stops being where thinking happens and becomes where thinking is guarded. Sometimes the machine misunderstands him in a more useful way than understanding would. Sometimes it hands back something smooth and completely dead — a reminder that polish and life are two different things.

The phrase we have — written with AI — covers four different things. A student pastes in a prompt and submits what comes back. A novelist runs a finished chapter through a model to catch repeated words. A journalist has a machine draft the middle third and tells nobody. And whatever Moss is doing. Fraud, copy editing, hiding — and a fourth with no name, so readers file it under one of the other three. Hearing a machine's tone cannot tell them apart.

The better questions, he says, are these. What did the person bring? What did the machine add? What did the result become that neither would have made alone? Under those sits one he cannot answer. Can that accounting be done at all — or does enough back-and-forth finally produce a thought with no ledger to check it against, one that was never sitting on either side to begin with?

sections.label: Steelman
sections.text: The oldest objection has a strong form. A sampler has no hands and no taste. It does not know why four particular bars matter enough to loop. So what comes out is the machine's work wearing a musician's name. Moss spent thirty years in music hearing that about his own records, and hears the same charge about his sentences now. His answer: it turned out to be a claim about a technology, not about any one piece of work, and he thinks it still is. That is a bet, not a proof.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: How typical is this? It is one writer describing his own method, in an essay made by that method, with no outside check. He never shows which sentences came from where — and by his own last paragraph, he is not sure that could be shown. He also brings thirty years of building music out of material someone else made. Most writers do not have that training, which may make his case unusually clean rather than typical. Even the editor's note introducing the column was machine-written and human-edited. Read it as one careful case, not a survey.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: "Being right was never the point. Having something there to answer back was."

recall.q: Moss's editor said two things at once: the prose sounds machine-made, and the ideas are clearly Moss's own. Why does Moss think "did AI write this?" cannot settle that?
recall.a: Because that question lumps four different practices together — the student who submits a chatbot's output, the novelist using a model as a copy editor, the journalist hiding a machine-drafted middle, and Moss's own back-and-forth. Hearing a machine's tone tells you nothing about what the person brought or what survived their judgment.

cards.title: Why W is called double U: it really was two Us
cards.body: Latin had no letter for the sound that starts water, because Latin had lost the sound itself. Germanic scribes patched the hole by writing U twice, and by the 11th century the pair had fused into one letter. Back then U and V were still the same letter. That is why English calls the shape double U.

sections.text:
A scribe in Francia, writing Latin in the 500s, reaches a king's name and stops. The name holds a sound — the one that starts water and want — and the Latin alphabet has no letter for it. So the scribe writes U twice and carries on.

That quick fix is the last letter of your alphabet. Every other letter is named for a noise: ay, bee, see. W is named for how it was built.

The gap came first. Latin and Greek both once had the w-sound, and both had letters for it. Both lost it. In Latin, V slid over to stand for the v-sound instead. By the fifth century Latin had neither the sound nor a sign for it.

Then the western empire came apart. The last emperor there was pushed out in 476, and Germanic rulers held land from southern Spain to the North Sea. They wanted to look Roman, so they kept Latin for official papers — and handed their scribes names packed with the w-sound: Clovis, Vitiges, Odoacer.

The doubled U spread from the 500s, probably out of Francia. An abbot appears in the records as UUandeberctus, a king as UUaldemarus. The two letters crept closer together and, by the 11th century, had fused. All of this happened before U and V split into separate letters. That is why English says double U while the French say double vé.

England went its own way for a while. Latin written there used the doubled U: a tenth-century life of Bishop Æthelwold spells him Aðeluuoldus, among Winchester, Worcester and Wallingford. But writers putting down English, not Latin, felt freer. They borrowed a rune instead: Ƿ, called wynn. It appears twice in the first line of our only surviving copy of Beowulf. Wessex scribes wrote tƿa and ƿord. Someone carved it on a decorated dagger, later found in Kent.

Wynn survived the Norman Conquest, then faded through the Middle English centuries. French and Latin had used W since the 500s, and the pressure to match them won. Those scribes also hit a practical snag: W beside U made a picket fence of upright strokes that all looked the same. So they swapped the U for an O. That is why wulf, wud and wunder are now wolf, wood and wonder — a handwriting fix, frozen in place.

W kept taking on new work. A soft G inside Old English words slid into the w-sound: fugol became fowl, sagu became saw. In town, cow and owl — once tun, cu and ule — W is not a consonant at all. It is a flag that the vowel has shifted.

It also bends what follows. The w-sound is made with rounded lips, and it rounds the vowel beside it, dragging it backwards in the mouth. The change is recent: Shakespeare rhymed was with glass, Byron still rhymed wand with hand. Spelling never caught up. We could write woz and wond. Perhaps one day we will.

sections.label: See it in your life
items: Say as, has, was. The first two rhyme. The third does not — the W has rounded the vowel and pulled it back.
The same split, every time: and, hand, wand. Arm, harm, warm. Ash, bash, wash. Fan against swan, far against war, fat against what.
The letter is not needed, only the sound. Quartz is spelled with a QU, and it rhymes with shorts, not with parts.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The alphabet is not a design. It is a stack of small fixes nobody got around to undoing.

recall.q: W is called double U, but the shape we write looks like two Vs. Why the mismatch?
recall.a: Because the letter really was two Us, written in an age when U and V were still one and the same letter. English kept that older name. French, naming the same shape, says double vé.

cards.title: Hidden self-doubt spots anger and disgust sooner
cards.body: People low in hidden self-esteem caught anger and disgust on a slowly changing face at much weaker intensity than others. What they said about themselves on a questionnaire stopped predicting anything once that hidden layer was counted. Seeing disgust early also came with worse relationships.
cards.evidence: single study · n=225 adults · lab detection task + Implicit Association Test · correlational, 4–7% of variance

sections.text:
Press the key the moment you see the feeling arrive. On the screen, a face sits blank. Then it shifts two percent toward an emotion. Then two percent more, and more, until it is fully angry — or disgusted, or afraid, or happy. Two hundred and twenty-five adults watched these slow changes and tapped as soon as they could name what was forming. The fastest ones catch a curled lip or a tight jaw while it is still almost nothing.

First, everyone answered a normal self-esteem questionnaire — do you feel you have a number of good qualities, that kind of question. Psychologists call this explicit self-esteem: the view of yourself you can say out loud. Then came an Implicit Association Test. It is a speed game: you sort self-words and other-words into good and bad piles as fast as you can. If self-words drop into the good pile faster, your implicit self-esteem counts as high. That is the automatic layer, running under the sentence you would write about yourself.

The two layers often disagree. A person can tick every confident box and still be slow to pair themselves with anything good. Another can report feeling worthless while the automatic sorting says otherwise. That gap has a name: self-esteem discrepancy.

The lower a person's implicit self-esteem, the less of an expression they needed to catch anger and disgust. They were faster on fear too. A wide gap between the two layers did the same thing, and the direction of the gap did not matter. Fine out loud but doubting underneath, or low out loud but fine underneath — both spotted anger and disgust early.

At first, the questionnaire score did look like it predicted how early anger was spotted. That link vanished once implicit self-esteem entered the model. Older work blamed low conscious self-esteem for rejection sensitivity; it may have been reading the automatic layer underneath. The questionnaire still mattered elsewhere. It tracked wellbeing strongly.

Early detection was not tied to overall wellbeing. It split. People quick to see disgust reported worse relations with others. People quick to see anger scored higher on autonomy — usually a good word, but the authors read it here as distance. If you catch the first flicker of someone turning on you, one way to stay safe is to need them less.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text:
These are correlations, and small ones. The automatic layer and the gap explained about 4 to 7 percent of the differences between people in anger and disgust sensitivity. Nothing here shows that a self-esteem profile causes anyone to see rejection sooner.

The lead author is firm that the sorting test does not uncover a hidden "true" self-esteem. It measures automatic links to the self, and other methods need to repeat the result. Spotting a faint expression on a screen is also not the same as feeling rejected by a real person. This study measured seeing, not rejection sensitivity as a trait.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: You can only report the self-esteem you know about. The face on the screen is being read by the other one.

recall.q: Conscious self-esteem looked at first like it predicted how early people spotted anger. What happened to that link?
recall.a: It vanished once implicit self-esteem and the gap between the two layers were counted. So older findings that blamed low conscious self-esteem for rejection sensitivity may have been tracking the automatic layer underneath.

cards.title: Two depression drugs, the same change in reading faces
cards.body: Psilocybin and a common daily antidepressant both made patients less likely to see anger or sadness in a face — and by about the same amount. But only in the antidepressant group did that change predict how depressed people felt a month later. Brain scans had already shown the two drugs working through different machinery.
cards.evidence: single study · n=59 · randomized, double-blind · secondary analysis · self-report depression scores

sections.text:
Half a second, and the face is gone. Six feelings were possible — anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness, surprise. The face may have been at full strength, or so faint it was almost blank. Press the key. Name what you saw.

Depressed people miss in one direction on this test. They read the anger and the sadness accurately. The faint happiness slips past them, or comes back as something worse. Psychiatry calls this a negative affective bias: a habit of reading the unclear parts of the world as hostile. Models of depression treat it as a cause, not a side effect. Mood bends what you see, and what you see feeds the mood.

That loop is the standard explanation for something strange about ordinary antidepressants. SSRIs — selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, the common daily pills, escitalopram among them — take weeks to lift mood. The theory says the drug tilts what you see first. Mood catches up later, after weeks of living in a world that looks a little less against you.

Psilocybin, the active ingredient in magic mushrooms, does not take weeks. Trials show it easing symptoms fast. Marieke Martens and colleagues at Oxford asked whether it gets there by the same road: 59 people with long-standing, moderate-to-severe depression, six weeks, psilocybin or escitalopram, the face test at the start and at the end.

Both groups came out less negative, by about the same amount. After six weeks, patients in both groups were less accurate at spotting negative emotions than at the start, and misread fewer faces as negative. They also got faster — and by the end, faster at happy faces than at negative ones. The gap between the two drugs was too small to separate from chance.

Brain scans of these same patients had already shown the drugs doing different things. Escitalopram quieted the amygdala — a small brain area that handles fear and threat — while patients looked at faces. Psilocybin did not. Same behaviour on the test, different machinery underneath.

Then the split widened. At six weeks, the change in bias lined up with nothing: in neither group did a bigger drop in negativity come with a bigger drop in depression scores. But at ten weeks, a month later, the escitalopram group's earlier change paid off. The patients who had stopped misreading happy faces as negative were the ones now scoring lower on depression. That is the SSRI theory doing exactly what it predicts.

The psilocybin group showed no such link. Their bias moved, but how far it moved told you nothing about their depression scores a month later. Whatever makes psilocybin work fast, this study suggests, it is probably not the slow retraining of how a face looks.

sections.label: The experiment
sections.text:
Fifty-nine patients, split at random into two groups, six weeks. One group got two 25-milligram doses of psilocybin, three weeks apart, plus a dummy pill daily. The other got escitalopram daily, plus two one-milligram doses of psilocybin as a placebo, so the dosing days felt the same from the inside. Neither the patients nor the clinicians knew who was on which.

Both groups got the same psychological support: preparation before each dosing session, and integration sessions afterwards to talk it through. The face test ran at the start and at six weeks. Depression was measured by questionnaire at six weeks and again at ten.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text:
No group went without an active drug. So the chemistry cannot be cleanly separated from the therapy every patient got.

The researchers also expect their volunteers leaned one way: people who join a psychedelic trial often want the psilocybin, and that hope can colour how they respond and how they report it. And the ten-week result is a correlation inside one group — a pattern, not proof of cause. Next time the team plans to test patients within days of dosing, to see how fast the shift really arrives.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Two drugs can hand you the same kinder face and still not be doing the same work.

recall.q: Both groups' negative bias dropped by about the same amount. So what was different between the two drugs?
recall.a: Only in the escitalopram group did the six-week drop in bias predict lower depression scores four weeks later. In the psilocybin group the bias moved but told you nothing about later mood — a hint that psilocybin's fast relief works some other way.

cards.title: How often a child blinks tracks their mental flexibility
cards.body: Spontaneous blinking — the kind you never notice yourself doing — is thought to reflect the brain's dopamine system. In 113 children aged three to six, the ones who blinked more did better at a rule-switching card game. And the link ran through one small patch of prefrontal cortex. An ordinary camera picked up something researchers assumed needed a scanner.
cards.evidence: single study · n=113 · ages 35–80 months · fNIRS + video blink counts · correlational

sections.text:
A four-year-old sits at a table with a pile of cards. Sort them by colour, says the researcher — red here, blue there. The child does it. Then the rule changes: now sort by shape. Rabbits here, boats there. For a young child this is genuinely hard. Many keep sorting by colour while saying the new rule out loud.

That small failure is one of psychology's cleanest tests of executive function — the mental controls that let you hold a rule in mind, stop an old habit, and adapt. It arrives fast between ages three and six. How well it arrives predicts school results, social skill, even physical and emotional health much later.

So researchers want to watch the brain while it happens. The obstacle is the equipment. The strongest imaging, like MRI, is too confining and too frightening for many young children — and especially for the clinical groups who most need studying. Which is why one team went looking for something a camera could measure.

They chose blinking. Not deliberate blinking, but the spontaneous kind that happens outside awareness. How often you blink is thought to be shaped by the brain's neuromodulator systems — chemicals that tune whole circuits rather than carry one message — and by dopamine in particular. Its growth curve is suspicious, too. Newborns blink only a few times a minute. The rate climbs through infancy toward the adult 20 to 30 a minute, just as executive function is firming up.

So: 113 children, roughly three to six years old, doing the card-switch task. Ordinary video cameras counted their blinks. At the same time, sensors resting gently on the scalp recorded activity in the prefrontal cortex — functional near-infrared spectroscopy, no scanner, no tube.

The children who blinked more did better at switching. That still held after the researchers accounted for age, so this was not just older-and-therefore-better.

Then the brain data narrowed it. A higher blink rate was not tied to general alertness, or to the prefrontal cortex broadly. It tracked one place: the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, the same patch that handles rule-switching in adults. No other subregion they measured showed the link. And older children used that patch in a more focused way — what the authors call greater "functional differentiation", a brain handing the job to fewer, more specialised circuits instead of lighting up everywhere. Blink rate rises alongside that sharpening.

That is what makes the result useful rather than merely odd. If a count taken from routine video tracks a circuit that deep, executive development could be followed in exactly the children who are hardest to put inside a machine. The authors say the next step is testing that in clinical groups, to see whether a blink rate can flag neurodevelopmental conditions early. It has not been shown yet.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text:
This is one study, and it is correlational — things moved together, which is not the same as one causing the other. Blink rate went with better switching and with right-dlPFC activity. Nothing here shows blinking causes either, or that making a child blink more would change anything.

The dopamine link is inferred, not measured. The researchers say spontaneous blinking is thought to be influenced by neuromodulator systems. That is not the same as watching dopamine in these children.

And there is no threshold. The work compares children across a group. It says nothing about what any single child's blink rate means.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Something chemical, in a place too deep to see, leaves a trace on the outside of a face — and you can count it.

recall.q: Blink rate did not track the prefrontal cortex in general. Which single spot did it track, and why does that specificity matter?
recall.a: The right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex — the same patch that handles rule-switching in adults, and no other subregion they measured. Because the link is that precise, a blink count from ordinary video could stand in for a deep circuit in children who cannot be put inside a scanner.

cards.title: India studies a US law that targets Russian-oil buyers
cards.body: A new US law allows tariffs of up to 100% on countries that buy Russian oil and gas. The tariff does not land on the oil. It lands on everything those countries sell to America. India is one of the big buyers named, and Piyush Goyal says the government is still reading the details.

sections.text:
A new American law lets Washington put tariffs of up to 100% on countries that buy Russian oil and gas. It takes effect within thirty days. On 21 September, Piyush Goyal said India is still studying the details.

The penalty does not touch the oil trade. It falls on what the buying country sells to the United States. India and China are named among the big buyers of Russian energy. Both could face much higher duties on their exports to America — goods with no link to crude.

The law allows the tariff; it does not order it. It does not say which countries go on the list, or when.

sections.label: The numbers
items: Up to 100% — the highest tariff the new US law allows on buyers of Russian oil and gas
30 days — the wait before the law takes effect
India and China — the big buyers named as facing possible higher duties on their US exports
21 September 2026 — Goyal's statement that India is still studying the details

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: An Indian exporter of textiles, machinery or shrimp does not choose where the country buys its oil. The cost would still reach their door, because the tariff is charged on the country, not on the barrel.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: Whether Washington uses the power once the thirty days run out, and which countries it names first. Until then India's position is one word: studying.

recall.q: The new US law is aimed at countries that buy Russian oil. So what would the tariff actually be charged on?
recall.a: Not the oil. It would fall on goods the buying country sells to the United States — so Indian exporters with no link to crude would carry the cost. And the law only allows the tariff; it does not order it.
